quests.questionSentence: The clause that the lawyer who drafted the agreement inserted at the last minute caused confusion. What did the lawyer insert?
quests.targetClause: the clause
quests.completedSentence: The clause that the lawyer who drafted the agreement inserted at the last minute caused confusion. What did the lawyer insert?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The clause' is what was inserted; 'that the lawyer ... inserted' is an object relative clause about the clause, with 'who drafted the agreement' nested inside it, describing the lawyer.
quests.nativeTip: There are two nested clauses here. Strip out 'who drafted the agreement' - it just tells you which lawyer. What was actually inserted?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the clause"

quests.questionSentence: In 'The clause that the lawyer who drafted the agreement inserted caused confusion,' which words form the clause describing 'the lawyer'?
quests.targetClause: who drafted the agreement
quests.completedSentence: In 'The clause that the lawyer who drafted the agreement inserted caused confusion,' which words form the clause describing 'the lawyer'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who drafted the agreement' is nested inside the larger clause 'that the lawyer ... inserted,' which itself describes 'the clause.' Each relative clause attaches to the noun immediately before its relative word.
quests.nativeTip: Find the relative word that comes directly after 'the lawyer' and see where that inner clause ends.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "who drafted the agreement"

quests.questionSentence: Which rewrite of the contract sentence is clearest, keeping the same meaning?
quests.targetClause: The lawyer drafted the agreement. The clause she inserted at the last minute caused confusion.
quests.completedSentence: Which rewrite of the contract sentence is clearest, keeping the same meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: Splitting the sentence keeps each clause next to its own noun and removes the nesting entirely, without changing the meaning. The other options either drop information or scramble the structure.
quests.nativeTip: Nested clauses can often be split into two shorter sentences without losing any information.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The lawyer drafted the agreement. The clause she inserted at the last minute caused confusion."

quests.questionSentence: The engineer confirmed that the bridge which the survey that the council commissioned had flagged as unsafe would be closed. What had been flagged as unsafe?
quests.targetClause: the bridge
quests.completedSentence: The engineer confirmed that the bridge which the survey that the council commissioned had flagged as unsafe would be closed. What had been flagged as unsafe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The bridge' is what the survey flagged as unsafe. 'That the council commissioned' is nested inside, describing 'the survey,' and the whole thing sits inside the clause describing 'the bridge.'
quests.nativeTip: Peel back the layers one at a time: a survey was commissioned, and that survey flagged something. What did it flag?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the bridge"

quests.questionSentence: In the same sentence, what is the grammatical role of 'the council' inside its own small clause?
quests.targetClause: The subject of 'commissioned'
quests.completedSentence: In the same sentence, what is the grammatical role of 'the council' inside its own small clause?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The council' is the subject of 'commissioned' - the council commissioned the survey. This is the innermost of the three nested clauses in the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Find the verb 'commissioned' and ask who performed that action.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The subject of 'commissioned'"

quests.questionSentence: Which plain-language rewrite keeps the same meaning as the nested original?
quests.targetClause: The council commissioned a survey. The survey flagged the bridge as unsafe. The bridge will be closed.
quests.completedSentence: Which plain-language rewrite keeps the same meaning as the nested original?
quests.ruleExplanation: This version keeps the same three facts in the same logical order without nesting: the council commissioned a survey, the survey flagged the bridge, and the bridge will close. The other rewrites change or lose information.
quests.nativeTip: Unpack the layers in order: who commissioned what, what that thing found, and what will happen as a result.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The council commissioned a survey. The survey flagged the bridge as unsafe. The bridge will be closed."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Attachment Ambiguity in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: She interviewed the parents of the students who had complained. Who had complained?
quests.targetClause: It is ambiguous - most readers would assume 'the students,' but 'the parents' is also grammatically possible.
quests.completedSentence: She interviewed the parents of the students who had complained. Who had complained?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who had complained' most naturally attaches to the nearer noun, 'the students,' since nothing marks it as referring to 'the parents.' Because both nouns could take a plural verb, this sentence is genuinely ambiguous without more context.
quests.nativeTip: Check the verb's number and think about which reading a reader would naturally assume without more context.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "It is ambiguous - most readers would assume 'the students,' but 'the parents' is also grammatically possible."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Attachment Ambiguity in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which rewrite removes the ambiguity and makes clear that the PARENTS complained?
quests.targetClause: She interviewed the parents, who had complained, of the students.
quests.completedSentence: Which rewrite removes the ambiguity and makes clear that the PARENTS complained?
quests.ruleExplanation: Placing the clause right after 'the parents' leaves no doubt about who complained. The other options either keep the ambiguity or scramble the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Move the clause so it sits directly next to 'parents' instead of 'students.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "She interviewed the parents, who had complained, of the students."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Attachment Ambiguity in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which rewrite is the clearest way to say the STUDENTS complained, avoiding any of the original ambiguity?
quests.targetClause: She interviewed the parents of students who had complained.
quests.completedSentence: Which rewrite is the clearest way to say the STUDENTS complained, avoiding any of the original ambiguity?
quests.ruleExplanation: Naming 'the students who had complained' first and then adding their parents removes the ambiguity entirely. The other versions either keep both readings open or are grammatically broken.
quests.nativeTip: Give 'students' its own short clause before folding in the parents, so there is no doubt about who is doing the complaining.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "She interviewed the parents of students who had complained."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: The airline cancelled the flight, which stranded hundreds of passengers overnight. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.targetClause: the fact that the airline cancelled the flight
quests.completedSentence: The airline cancelled the flight, which stranded hundreds of passengers overnight. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' refers to the whole event of cancelling the flight, not to 'the flight' alone - a flight cannot strand anyone by simply existing, but cancelling one can.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what actually stranded the passengers - the flight itself, or the fact that it was cancelled?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the fact that the airline cancelled the flight"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence uses 'which' to refer to a single noun rather than a whole clause?
quests.targetClause: The airline grounded the plane, which needed repairs.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence uses 'which' to refer to a single noun rather than a whole clause?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The plane, which needed repairs' attaches 'which' to the single noun 'plane.' In the delay and rebooking sentences, 'which' points back to the whole preceding event rather than one noun.
quests.nativeTip: In one of these sentences, something specific 'needed repairs' - a plane, not an event.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The airline grounded the plane, which needed repairs."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The flight was cancelled, that stranded hundreds of passengers.'
quests.targetClause: 'That' cannot follow a comma or refer to a whole preceding clause; 'which' is needed.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The flight was cancelled, that stranded hundreds of passengers.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never follow a comma, and it also cannot refer back to a whole clause the way 'which' can. 'Which' is required here.
quests.nativeTip: This 'which' refers to a whole event, not a single noun. Check which pronoun is allowed to do that job.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'That' cannot follow a comma or refer to a whole preceding clause; 'which' is needed."

quests.questionSentence: Which review sentence makes clear that the STAFF (not the food) were unfriendly?
quests.targetClause: The staff, who were unfriendly, ruined an otherwise good meal.
quests.completedSentence: Which review sentence makes clear that the STAFF (not the food) were unfriendly?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The staff, who were unfriendly, ruined an otherwise good meal' places the clause directly after 'staff.' In the other options the clause drifts toward 'meal' or is missing its comma.
quests.nativeTip: Keep the clause describing the staff right next to the word 'staff.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The staff, who were unfriendly, ruined an otherwise good meal."

quests.questionSentence: A product review says: 'I bought a charger for my laptop that stopped working after a week.' What is ambiguous here?
quests.targetClause: It is unclear whether the charger or the laptop stopped working.
quests.completedSentence: A product review says: 'I bought a charger for my laptop that stopped working after a week.' What is ambiguous here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That stopped working' sits right after 'laptop,' so it could describe either the laptop or the charger the reviewer meant to complain about. Moving the clause next to 'charger' would remove the ambiguity.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what could grammatically have 'stopped working' - the charger, or the laptop.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "It is unclear whether the charger or the laptop stopped working."

quests.questionSentence: Which rewrite of the charger review removes the ambiguity, making clear the CHARGER stopped working?
quests.targetClause: I bought a charger that stopped working after a week for my laptop.
quests.completedSentence: Which rewrite of the charger review removes the ambiguity, making clear the CHARGER stopped working?
quests.ruleExplanation: Moving the prepositional phrase after the clause keeps 'that stopped working' directly beside 'charger.' The other options keep the ambiguity or break the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Move 'for my laptop' so it no longer sits between 'charger' and its clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I bought a charger that stopped working after a week for my laptop."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause Preview (Recognition)
quests.questionSentence: The proposal submitted yesterday is already under review. What full relative clause is 'submitted yesterday' standing in for?
quests.targetClause: that was submitted yesterday
quests.completedSentence: The proposal submitted yesterday is already under review. What full relative clause is 'submitted yesterday' standing in for?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Submitted yesterday' is a shortened form of 'that was submitted yesterday' - the relative pronoun and 'was' have both been dropped, leaving only the past participle. You will study this pattern, called a reduced relative clause, in the levels ahead.
quests.nativeTip: Try inserting 'that/which was' right before 'submitted' and see if the sentence still makes sense.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that was submitted yesterday"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause Preview (Recognition)
quests.questionSentence: The team working on the merger meets every morning. What full relative clause does 'working on the merger' stand in for?
quests.targetClause: that is working on the merger
quests.completedSentence: The team working on the merger meets every morning. What full relative clause does 'working on the merger' stand in for?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Working on the merger' is short for 'that is working on the merger' - here the pronoun and 'is' have been dropped, leaving only the '-ing' form. This is the present-tense version of the same shortening pattern.
quests.nativeTip: Try inserting 'that/who is' right before 'working' and see if the meaning stays the same.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that is working on the merger"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Reduced Relative Clause Preview (Recognition)
quests.questionSentence: Both 'submitted yesterday' and 'working on the merger' are shortened relative clauses. What do they have in common?
quests.targetClause: In both, the relative pronoun and a form of 'be' have been dropped, leaving only the participle.
quests.completedSentence: Both 'submitted yesterday' and 'working on the merger' are shortened relative clauses. What do they have in common?
quests.ruleExplanation: In both cases, the relative pronoun and a form of 'be' have been dropped, leaving only the participle - a past participle for the passive version, an '-ing' form for the active one. You will explore exactly when this shortening is possible in an upcoming phase.
quests.nativeTip: Compare what has been removed from each one: a relative pronoun, and a form of the verb 'be.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "In both, the relative pronoun and a form of 'be' have been dropped, leaving only the participle."

quests.questionSentence: The results of the survey, the methodology of which had been criticised by peer reviewers, were nonetheless published. What had been criticised?
quests.targetClause: the survey's methodology
quests.completedSentence: The results of the survey, the methodology of which had been criticised by peer reviewers, were nonetheless published. What had been criticised?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Of which' points back to 'the survey': the survey's methodology was criticised. 'The results' is what got published, not what was criticised.
quests.nativeTip: 'The methodology of which' - whose methodology is this referring to?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the survey's methodology"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The committee reviewed the proposals, several of which ___ later withdrawn by their authors.
quests.targetClause: were
quests.completedSentence: The committee reviewed the proposals, several of which were later withdrawn by their authors.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Several' is plural, so the verb must be 'were.' The plural noun 'proposals' inside 'of which' does not itself control the verb - the quantifier does.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the quantifier 'several' - is it singular or plural?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "were"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly reports that only some of the committee's recommendations were adopted, not all of them?
quests.targetClause: The recommendations that the board approved were implemented within a month.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly reports that only some of the committee's recommendations were adopted, not all of them?
quests.ruleExplanation: Without commas, 'that the board approved' is defining and narrows the group down to only the approved recommendations. With commas, the sentence would claim the board approved every recommendation.
quests.nativeTip: Decide whether the clause should narrow down which recommendations were adopted, or simply describe all of them.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The recommendations that the board approved were implemented within a month."

quests.questionSentence: The email from the vendor whose invoice had already been paid confused the accounting team. Whose invoice had been paid?
quests.targetClause: the vendor
quests.completedSentence: The email from the vendor whose invoice had already been paid confused the accounting team. Whose invoice had been paid?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' attaches to the nearest logical noun, 'the vendor,' so it is the vendor's invoice that had been paid. 'The email' cannot own an invoice.
quests.nativeTip: 'Whose' points to the noun directly in front of it, not to a noun buried inside a prepositional phrase further back.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the vendor"

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is the clearest possible rewrite of the vendor/invoice sentence, keeping the same meaning?
quests.targetClause: The vendor's invoice had already been paid. The email about it confused the accounting team.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is the clearest possible rewrite of the vendor/invoice sentence, keeping the same meaning?
quests.ruleExplanation: Splitting the sentence keeps 'the vendor' and 'whose invoice' next to each other and removes any need to untangle a long noun phrase. The other options change the meaning or garble the grammar.
quests.nativeTip: Split the idea into two short sentences so nothing has to be untangled.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The vendor's invoice had already been paid. The email about it confused the accounting team."

quests.questionSentence: In 'The manager rejected the estimate that the contractor whose team was understaffed had submitted,' which clause is nested inside another?
quests.targetClause: 'whose team was understaffed' is nested inside 'that the contractor had submitted'
quests.completedSentence: In 'The manager rejected the estimate that the contractor whose team was understaffed had submitted,' which clause is nested inside another?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose team was understaffed' sits entirely inside the larger clause 'that the contractor ... had submitted,' which itself describes 'the estimate.' This is the same nesting pattern practised earlier in this phase.
quests.nativeTip: Look for a relative clause that sits entirely within the boundaries of a longer one.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'whose team was understaffed' is nested inside 'that the contractor had submitted'"

quests.questionSentence: The recall affects vehicles manufactured before 2019, which the company says pose a fire risk. What poses the fire risk?
quests.targetClause: the vehicles manufactured before 2019
quests.completedSentence: The recall affects vehicles manufactured before 2019, which the company says pose a fire risk. What poses the fire risk?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Vehicles' is the only noun that could logically pose a fire risk, and 'which' with a plural sense matches it; '2019' is just a year and cannot pose anything.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'vehicles' or '2019' can logically 'pose a fire risk,' and look at the verb's number.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the vehicles manufactured before 2019"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which safety notice sentence is correctly punctuated, given that only SOME vehicles in the fleet are affected?
quests.targetClause: Vehicles that were manufactured before 2019 must be inspected immediately.
quests.completedSentence: Which safety notice sentence is correctly punctuated, given that only SOME vehicles in the fleet are affected?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since only some vehicles are affected, the clause must narrow the group down, so it is defining: no commas, and 'that' works. With commas, the sentence would wrongly claim every vehicle in the fleet was manufactured before 2019.
quests.nativeTip: Decide whether the clause should narrow the group down to certain vehicles, or describe the whole fleet.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Vehicles that were manufactured before 2019 must be inspected immediately."

quests.questionSentence: In 'The regulator, whose warning the company had ignored for months, opened a formal investigation,' what is the grammatical role of 'the company'?
quests.targetClause: The subject of 'had ignored'
quests.completedSentence: In 'The regulator, whose warning the company had ignored for months, opened a formal investigation,' what is the grammatical role of 'the company'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The company' is the subject of 'had ignored' - the company ignored the regulator's warning. 'Whose' simply supplies the possessive link between 'the regulator' and 'warning.'
quests.nativeTip: Find the verb 'had ignored' and ask who performed that action.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The subject of 'had ignored'"

quests.questionSentence: The findings of the panel that reviewed the complaints filed by former employees were released Friday. What was released?
quests.targetClause: the findings
quests.completedSentence: The findings of the panel that reviewed the complaints filed by former employees were released Friday. What was released?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The findings' - a plural noun matching the plural verb 'were released' - is what was released. 'The panel,' 'the complaints,' and 'former employees' are all part of the descriptive chain leading up to it, not the antecedent.
quests.nativeTip: Two decoys and a nested clause sit between the true antecedent and 'were released.' Check the verb's number and work backward.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the findings"

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence removes the ambiguity in 'They fired the manager who oversaw the department that failed the audit,' making clear the DEPARTMENT failed the audit (which is already true), while also making clear who was fired?
quests.targetClause: The manager oversaw a department that failed the audit. The company fired the manager.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence removes the ambiguity in 'They fired the manager who oversaw the department that failed the audit,' making clear the DEPARTMENT failed the audit (which is already true), while also making clear who was fired?
quests.ruleExplanation: This rewrite keeps both facts in order without nesting: the manager oversaw the department, and the department failed the audit, and then the firing is reported. The other options blur or reverse who did what.
quests.nativeTip: The original is actually unambiguous once you check verb agreement - but rewrite it as two clear sentences to confirm your understanding of both nested clauses.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The manager oversaw a department that failed the audit. The company fired the manager."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Attachment Ambiguity in Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which statement about complex, real-world relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.targetClause: A relative clause always attaches to the very first noun in the sentence, no matter how far away it is.
quests.completedSentence: Which statement about complex, real-world relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.ruleExplanation: A relative clause almost always attaches to the noun closest to it, or to whichever noun the verb's number logically supports - it does not simply attach to the first noun in the sentence regardless of distance or agreement. The other three statements are true.
quests.nativeTip: Test each statement against what this block has taught about nesting, ambiguity, and whole-clause reference.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "A relative clause always attaches to the very first noun in the sentence, no matter how far away it is."
